description: Cranial morphology dimensions visible from photograph: cephalic index (head shape from above), cranial profile in sagittal view, occipital morphology, head circumference proxy. **Important framing note:** these dimensions use contemporary craniofacial-anthropology vocabulary developed for clinical applications such as craniosynostosis screening and pediatric-orthotic assessment. They are explicitly **not** the discredited 19th-century racial-typology cranial measurements that conflated cephalic index with hierarchical population claims (Boas's own 1912 work showed cephalic index changes within a generation under different environments, undermining its use as a stable racial marker). Modern usage treats cephalic index as a developmental and clinical descriptor with substantial individual variation and meaningful but partial population-level differences. The dimensions below capture the photo-observable shape variation; users should resist any interpretation that maps directly onto historical racial categorizations.

reliability_studies.method: test-retest: the identical prompt re-read against stored codings, same model, no human rater
reliability_studies.measures: reproducibility, NOT validity. Agreement between two readings says the instrument is stable, not that it is correct.
reliability_studies.corpus: publicly documented portraits of notable people, 39 ethnic groups, single frontal or three-quarter images
reliability_studies.statistic: percent agreement and Cohen's kappa over portraits where both readings gave a non-decline value
reliability_studies.decline_handling: A value meaning "could not assess" (unclear, not_visible, not_assessable, obscured, covered_unclear, not_applicable_or_*) is treated as a decline, not an answer. Scoring declines as answers makes a dimension that is never visible look perfectly reliable.
limitations: One model, one corpus, one re-read. No human inter-rater study exists for this vocabulary.

Kappa is fragile wherever one value dominates. Measured on this corpus: six dimensions read kappa at or below zero on 78 portraits and between 0.43 and 0.66 on 196, and every one has chance agreement above 85 percent. Those carry estimate_is_fragile and should be read as a band, not a number.
Notable-people corpora skew older and are not a population sample.
A dimension can be perfectly reproducible and still not measure what its name claims.

dimensions.scale_citation: Cephalic index = (maximum head breadth / maximum head length) × 100. Modern clinical use: van Vlimmeren LA et al. (2007). Effect of pediatric physical therapy on deformational plagiocephaly. Archives of Pediatric and Adolescent Medicine. Boas F (1912) demonstrated environmental variability in cephalic index that undermines its use as a stable population-classification marker; included here as a continuous developmental dimension with explicit framing.
dimensions.description: Ratio of head breadth to head length, captured as ordinal buckets aligned with the standard clinical classification thresholds. Used in pediatric orthopedics for assessing positional plagiocephaly and brachycephaly, not as a population-classification tool.

values.definition: Cephalic index < ~76; head substantially longer than wide. Clinical context: scaphocephaly when severe in infants.
Cephalic index ~81-85; head substantially wider relative to length.
Cephalic index > ~85; pronounced width-to-length ratio. Clinical context: positional plagiocephaly in infants.
Hairstyle or framing prevents reliable head-shape assessment.

observability.notes: Best assessed from a top-down view, which is rarely available in standard photographs. Frontal and lateral views allow only crude approximation. Hair volume substantially affects perceived width; assessment confidence should reflect this.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with descriptors used in pediatric-craniofacial literature on occipital morphology.
dimensions.description: Shape of the occipital (back-of-head) region in lateral view.

values.definition: Smooth posterior curve; pronounced occipital prominence.
Reduced posterior projection; flatter occipital silhouette. Often correlated with brachycephalic cephalic index.
Pronounced posterior projection of the occiput; visible bulge.
Notable left-right asymmetry of the occipital region.

observability.notes: Best assessed from lateral or three-quarter view; hair coverage substantially affects assessment.

reliability.note: Chance agreement is high because one value dominates this corpus, so kappa is computed on a small (1 - pe) denominator and the estimate moves a long way on a few cells. Measured: between a 78-portrait and a 196-portrait read of the same corpus, dimensions in this regime moved by up to 0.68 of a kappa point, in both directions. Read the band, not the digits.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with descriptors used in pediatric-orthotic and craniosynostosis literature.
dimensions.description: Vertical height of the cranium from the supraorbital ridge to the vertex.

values.definition: Reduced cranial height; vertex sits close to the level of the supraorbital ridge plus a small margin.
Pronounced cranial height; vertex sits well above the supraorbital ridge. Associated with sagittal-suture craniosynostosis when extreme in infants; constitutional in adults.

reliability.note: Chance agreement is high because one value dominates this corpus, so kappa is computed on a small (1 - pe) denominator and the estimate moves a long way on a few cells. Measured: between a 78-portrait and a 196-portrait read of the same corpus, dimensions in this regime moved by up to 0.68 of a kappa point, in both directions. Read the band, not the digits.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with the descriptors used in pediatric-growth-curve literature; reliable measurement requires a tape measure across the maximum circumference.
dimensions.description: Overall head circumference relative to body proportions, captured qualitatively.

values.definition: Head appears small relative to body; clinical microcephaly when extreme in infants.
Head appears large relative to body; clinical macrocephaly when extreme.

observability.notes: Reliable assessment requires whole-body framing for proportional comparison; head-only photographs cannot resolve this dimension.

framing_caveats.historical_misuse: Cranial measurements were extensively misused in 19th- and early 20th-century anthropology to support hierarchical claims about populations. Boas's 1912 study demonstrated that cephalic index responds to environment within a single generation, undermining any use of cranial morphology as a fixed population marker. Contemporary craniofacial anthropology uses these dimensions as developmental, clinical, and individual descriptors; downstream consumers of this dataset should resist mapping cephalic-index categories onto racial or population-typological claims.
framing_caveats.intended_uses: Pediatric craniofacial assessment (craniosynostosis screening, positional plagiocephaly), forensic anthropology (individual identification), aesthetic-medicine assessment, and clinical phenotype characterization. Population-level distributions in this dataset are documented but should not be interpreted as defining or distinguishing populations.

references: Boas F (1912). Changes in bodily form of descendants of immigrants. American Anthropologist, 14(3): 530-562.
